intro: Terms that look alike are where multiple choice catches people. Compare them side by side, then drill: you get a statement and pick the term it describes.

terms.name: Muda
terms.means: Waste: activity that uses resources without adding value.
terms.tip: Muda is what gets thrown away.
clues: Errors, queues and rework use up resources without adding value.
A ticket that waits in a queue for two days is an example of this.
Activity that consumes resources and adds nothing for the customer.

terms.name: Mura
terms.means: Unevenness: irregular demand or workload.
terms.tip: Mura is the uneven part, and it is often the cause.
clues: Demand that arrives in unpredictable batches.
An unstable schedule is this, and it can cause overtime.
Irregular demand or an uneven workload.

terms.name: Muri
terms.means: Overburden: too much load on people or equipment.
terms.tip: Muri is the overload, for example overtime.
clues: Overtime that loads people too heavily.
Too much load on people or on equipment.
What an unstable schedule causes before errors and queues appear.

groups.title: Takt time, cycle time or lead time?

terms.name: Takt time
terms.means: The pace the customer demand requires: net available time ÷ customer demand.
terms.tip: Takt is calculated from demand. You do not measure it.
clues: 420 minutes ÷ 140 units a day gives 3 minutes per unit.
The required rhythm to match customer demand.
It is not an observed time: it comes from available time and demand.

terms.name: Cycle time
terms.means: What you observe: the time to complete one cycle, or the time between finished units.
terms.tip: Cycle time is measured at a station. Compare it with takt.
clues: A station needs 4 minutes per unit.
The observed time between consecutive completed units.
If it is longer than the takt time, one station cannot meet demand.

terms.name: Lead time
terms.means: Elapsed time from the customer's request to delivery, including all waiting.
terms.tip: Lead time includes the waiting. Touch time does not.
clues: The whole time from request to delivery, waiting included.
Waiting can take up most of it.
A request that spends 3 calendar days in the process has this.

groups.title: DPU, DPO, DPMO or defective-unit rate?

terms.name: DPU
terms.means: Total defects ÷ total units.
terms.tip: DPU counts defects per unit and ignores the opportunities.
clues: 40 defects in 500 forms gives 0.08.
Defects per unit, one form can have several.
It counts defects, not defective forms.

terms.name: DPO
terms.means: Total defects ÷ (units × opportunities per unit).
terms.tip: DPO divides by the number of chances for a defect.
clues: 40 defects, 500 forms and 4 opportunities each gives 0.02.
Defects per opportunity.
The step before the DPMO: multiply it by 1,000,000 to get the DPMO.

terms.name: DPMO
terms.means: DPO × 1,000,000: defects per million opportunities.
terms.tip: DPMO is not defective units per million.
clues: 20,000 for 40 defects in 500 forms with 4 opportunities each.
Defects per million chances for a defect.
The number behind the 3.4 benchmark of Six Sigma.

terms.name: Defective-unit rate
terms.means: Units with at least one defect ÷ units.
terms.tip: A unit counts once, however many defects it has.
clues: 35 of 500 forms contain defects: 7%.
A form with three defects still counts as one.
It differs from the DPU when one unit has several defects.

terms.name: Transportation
terms.means: Unnecessary movement of materials or information between places.
terms.tip: Transportation: things or information move. Motion: people move.
clues: A ticket is copied between three teams.
Materials or information are moved between places more than needed.
Information is handed over again and again between departments.

terms.name: Motion
terms.means: Unnecessary movement by a person.
terms.tip: Motion: a person moves.
clues: A worker walks to a distant printer.
People walk or reach more than the task needs.
Staff move around to find what they need.

terms.name: Overprocessing
terms.means: More work than needed.
terms.tip: Overprocessing: doing more than the customer asked for.
clues: The same data is entered twice.
A task gets more work than the customer needs.
Extra checks and steps that add nothing for the customer.

terms.name: Waiting
terms.means: Idle time.
terms.tip: Waiting: the work sits still.
clues: A ticket stays in a queue for two days.
Work or people stand idle until the next step is ready.
Time passes and nothing is being done on the request.

terms.name: Defects
terms.means: Errors and rework.
terms.tip: Defects: it has to be done again.
clues: A ticket is reopened because the first fix failed.
An employee corrects an error.
Mistakes and the rework they cause.

terms.name: Skills (unused talent)
terms.means: Not using employees' expertise and ideas.
terms.tip: Skills is the eighth waste, the S of TIMWOODS.
clues: An employee knows how to automate a task, but nobody asks.
Staff ideas and expertise stay unused.
The eighth waste in the eight-waste model.

terms.name: Inventory
terms.means: Excess work in progress, stock or pending tickets.
terms.tip: Inventory: too much waiting in the pile.
clues: Far too many tickets are pending.
More work in progress than the process can handle.
Stock or work that piles up between steps.

terms.name: Overproduction
terms.means: Producing too early or too much.
terms.tip: Overproduction: more or sooner than demand asks.
clues: Work is made before anyone needs it.
More is produced than is asked for.
Producing too early or in too large amounts.

terms.name: White Belt
terms.means: Awareness and basic terminology.
terms.tip: The lowest level: knows the words.
clues: Basic awareness of Lean Six Sigma and support for the improvement culture.
Knows the basic terminology.
Awareness is the whole job.

terms.name: Yellow Belt
terms.means: Takes part in improvement activities and data collection.
terms.tip: Yellow takes part, Green leads.
clues: Participates in improvement work and collects data.
Helps a project team without leading it.
Takes part in improvement activities.

terms.name: Green Belt
terms.means: Leads bounded projects, usually next to normal duties.
terms.tip: Green leads the project.
clues: Leading a defined process-improvement project.
Leads a bounded project alongside normal duties.
The typical project leader of this course.

terms.name: Black Belt
terms.means: Leads complex analytical projects and coaches Green Belts.
terms.tip: Black coaches Green Belts.
clues: Leads complex analytical projects.
Coaches the Green Belts.
More analytical expertise than a Green Belt.

terms.name: Master Black Belt
terms.means: Methodological expert and deployment coach.
terms.tip: Not a sponsor by definition.
clues: A technical coaching and deployment role.
The methods expert of the organisation.
Not by definition the project sponsor.

terms.name: Champion
terms.means: Senior leader who selects and supports projects, secures resources and removes barriers.
terms.tip: Champion = sponsor, a governance role, not a belt.
clues: A senior leader who selects and supports the projects.
Secures resources and removes barriers.
A governance role rather than a technical belt.

terms.name: Just-in-Time
terms.means: Produce what is needed when it is needed.
terms.tip: One of the two pillars of TPS.
clues: Production is coordinated with demand.
Produce exactly what is needed, when it is needed.
A pillar of TPS that must not be confused with merely keeping inventory low.

terms.name: Jidoka
terms.means: Build quality into the process and stop to deal with abnormalities.
terms.tip: The other pillar of TPS. Detection must lead to a reaction.
clues: Stops or signals an abnormal condition and triggers a response.
Quality is built into the process.
Detecting a problem without reacting is not enough.

terms.name: Heijunka
terms.means: Levelling production volume and mix.
terms.tip: Heijunka = levelling.
clues: Reduces peaks in volume and mix.
Smooths the workload where demand allows it.
Levelling that is no reason to ignore urgent work.

terms.name: Andon
terms.means: A visual or audible signal that asks for support.
terms.tip: Andon = the signal.
clues: A signal that calls for help when something is abnormal.
A visual or audible request for support.
It requests support when something abnormal happens.

terms.name: Kaizen
terms.means: Continuous, incremental improvement with the people who do the work.
terms.tip: Kaizen = many small improvements.
clues: Continuous incremental improvement.
Improvement that involves the staff doing the work.
Not a one-time large investment.

terms.name: Poka Yoke
terms.means: Error-proofing: make errors hard to make or easy to detect.
terms.tip: Poka Yoke = foolproof.
clues: A connector that only fits in the right orientation.
A form field that rejects invalid input.
Barcode validation.

terms.name: VOC
terms.means: Voice of the Customer: the customers' needs, expectations and experiences.
terms.tip: VOC = what the customer says and needs.
clues: Evidence from interviews, surveys, complaints and service logs.
What customers need and experience.
Customers' words, as opposed to what the organisation assumes.

terms.name: VOB
terms.means: Voice of the Business: strategic, financial, regulatory and operational priorities.
terms.tip: VOB = what the business needs.
clues: Strategic, financial, regulatory and operational priorities.
The organisation's own priorities.
The business case of a project charter is linked to it.

terms.name: CTQ
terms.means: Critical to Quality: a broad need turned into something observable and measurable.
terms.tip: A CTQ has a target, a unit and an owner.
clues: 90% of priority-2 tickets get an initial response within 4 business hours.
'Fast support' made specific and measurable.
It needs an operational definition, a target, a unit, a measurement method and an owner.

terms.name: DMAIC
terms.means: A structured project path for an existing process problem, in five phases.
terms.tip: DMAIC = a project, PDCA = a habit.
clues: Define, Measure, Analyze, Improve, Control.
The structured path of a Green Belt project.
Used for an existing process problem, with a start and an end.

terms.name: PDCA
terms.means: A repeating learning cycle for everyday and experimental improvement.
terms.tip: Complements DMAIC, does not compete with it.
clues: Plan a change and a prediction, do a small test, check, then act.
A repeating cycle for learning in everyday improvement.
Adopt, adapt or abandon is its last step.

terms.name: Tollgate
terms.means: A formal review at the end of a phase: the sponsor checks the evidence and authorises the next phase.
terms.tip: A tollgate is not a sixth phase.
clues: A phase-end evidence review and authorization decision.
The sponsor decides whether the project may go on to the next phase.
It is a review, not an additional DMAIC phase.

terms.name: Project charter
terms.means: The document with the business case, problem statement, goal, scope, team and timeline. Made in Define.
terms.tip: The charter belongs to the Define phase.
clues: Contains the business case, scope, stakeholders, team and timeline.
Its problem statement should not name a preferred solution.
Made in the Define phase.

terms.name: I-MR chart
terms.means: For individual continuous measurements.
terms.tip: One measurement at a time.
clues: Individual continuous measurements.
Each point is a single measurement.
Used when data does not come in subgroups.

terms.name: X-bar/R chart
terms.means: For rational subgroups.
terms.tip: Measurements in subgroups.
clues: Data that comes in rational subgroups.
Tracks the subgroup average and range.
Used when several measurements are taken together each time.

terms.name: p-chart
terms.means: For the proportion defective.
terms.tip: p = proportion.
clues: Weekly defective-form proportions.
The share of defective items.
The proportion defective in a sample.

terms.name: u-chart
terms.means: For defects per unit when the exposure varies.
terms.tip: u = defects per unit.
clues: Defects per unit, with a varying opportunity exposure.
Counts defects, not defective items, when sample sizes differ.
Defects per unit over time.

terms.name: 5S
terms.means: Sort, Set in Order, Shine, Standardize, Sustain.
terms.tip: 5S = the workplace.
clues: Remove what is not needed, label what is, clean, agree standards, keep it up.
A workplace method of five steps, some add Safety as a sixth.
Used for example to set up a training room.

terms.name: SMED
terms.means: Reduce changeover time by separating internal and external activities.
terms.tip: SMED = changeovers.
clues: Single-Minute Exchange of Die.
Move activities that need a shutdown to ones that can be done while running.
Aims for changeovers in single-digit minutes where feasible.

terms.name: TPM
terms.means: Total Productive Maintenance: proactive and planned maintenance with operator involvement.
terms.tip: TPM = maintenance.
clues: Operators do safe basic care, specialists do the rest.
Proactive maintenance and systematic loss reduction.
Combines planned and quality maintenance.

terms.name: Kanban
terms.means: Visualizes work and limits work in progress (a pull system).
terms.tip: Kanban = visible WIP limits.
clues: Cards or columns that show work and limit WIP.
Explicit WIP limits expose blocked work.
A pull mechanism that authorises work from downstream consumption.

terms.name: Hoshin Kanri
terms.means: Policy deployment: strategy turned into goals, owners and review cycles.
terms.tip: Hoshin Kanri = strategy deployment, with catchball.
clues: Translates strategic priorities into a few breakthrough goals.
Uses catchball, a dialogue across levels.
Deployment and alignment of strategy with operational objectives.

terms.name: OEE
terms.means: Availability × Performance × Quality.
terms.tip: OEE = how well equipment is used.
clues: Three factors multiplied.
Measures how effectively equipment is used.
Has the six big losses behind it.

terms.name: FPY
terms.means: First-pass yield: units passing a process step without rework ÷ units entering.
terms.tip: FPY belongs to one step.
clues: Units that pass a step first time divided by units entering it.
The yield of one process step.
One of the factors in the rolled throughput yield.

terms.name: RTY
terms.means: Rolled throughput yield: the product of the step first-pass yields.
terms.tip: RTY multiplies the steps.
clues: Multiply the yields of all the steps.
Must not be guessed from the final inspection alone.
Three steps of 95%, 98% and 90% give a lower number than any of them.

terms.name: FTR
terms.means: First Time Right: work completed correctly without rework on the first attempt ÷ units processed × 100%.
terms.tip: FTR is the share done right the first time.
clues: Completing work correctly without rework on the first attempt.
Define whether reopening and exceptions count as failures.
910 of 1,000 tickets that never reopened gives 91%.

terms.name: 5 Whys
terms.means: Keep asking why, with evidence for every answer.
terms.tip: Five is a mnemonic, not a rule.
clues: Repeatedly ask why a condition occurred.
Stop when the causes are evidenced and actionable.
Does not have to ask exactly five questions.

terms.name: Fishbone (Ishikawa)
terms.means: Organises possible causes on branches, with the problem at the head.
terms.tip: It organises hypotheses, it proves nothing.
clues: The problem is the fish's head, causes are the bones.
Typical categories are Manpower, Machine, Method, Material, Measurement and Environment.
Also called a cause-and-effect diagram.

terms.name: Pareto analysis
terms.means: Ranks categories by frequency, cost or severity and shows the cumulative total.
terms.tip: The 80/20 rule is a rule of thumb.
clues: Ranks causes and shows the cumulative contribution.
Prioritise on impact and feasibility, not on frequency alone.
The 80/20 heuristic belongs to it.

terms.name: A3
terms.means: A concise one-page narrative from background to follow-up.
terms.tip: A3 = one page.
clues: Background, current condition, target, analysis, countermeasures, follow-up on one page.
Encourages evidence, shared thinking and coaching.
A one-page problem-solving story.

terms.name: FMEA
terms.means: Looks ahead at failure modes, effects, causes and controls. RPN = S × O × D.
terms.tip: FMEA is about risk, before it happens.
clues: Scores severity, occurrence and detectability.
A high-severity risk deserves attention even when the RPN is modest.
Anticipates failure modes and their effects.

terms.name: Service Value System element
terms.means: One of the five core elements: Guiding principles, Governance, Service value chain, Practices, Continual improvement.
terms.tip: 5 elements.
clues: Guiding principles is one of these.
Governance is one of these.
The service value chain is one of these.
Continual improvement is one of these.

terms.name: ITIL dimension
terms.means: One of the four dimensions: Organizations & people, Information & technology, Partners & suppliers, Value streams & processes.
terms.tip: 4 dimensions.
clues: Partners & suppliers is one of these.
Organizations & people is one of these.
Information & technology is one of these.
Value streams & processes is one of these.

terms.name: Lean
terms.means: Improves customer value and flow by reducing non-value-adding work.
terms.tip: Lean = waste and flow.
clues: Asks where time, effort and resources are wasted across the value stream.
Emphasises value, flow and waste reduction.
Its five principles run from value to perfection.

terms.name: Six Sigma
terms.means: Reduces defects and unwanted variation through measurement and analysis.
terms.tip: Six Sigma = defects and variation.
clues: Asks how reliably the process meets requirements.
Emphasises defects, variation and process capability.
Its benchmark is about 3.4 DPMO.

terms.name: Agile/Scrum
terms.means: A software delivery approach, not a definition of Lean.
terms.tip: Can coexist with Lean process improvement.
clues: A way to deliver software, like waterfall, but iterative.
Not an alternative definition of Lean.
Can exist side by side with Lean process improvement.
